unit.title: Geometry, Measurement & Scale
unit.essential_question: How do measurement, angle relationships, scale, coordinate reasoning, and geometric formulas support accurate and responsible design?
big_ideas: Measurements require appropriate units, tools, precision, and attention to error.
Angle and polygon relationships reveal geometric structure.
Perimeter, area, surface area, and volume answer different design questions and use different units.
Scale and similarity preserve shape while changing length, perimeter, area, and volume in predictable ways.
Right triangles and coordinates support distance, construction, navigation, and verification.
Geometric models are trustworthy only when constraints, assumptions, tolerances, and limitations are explicit.
unit.architecture: Open-age integrated Pre-Algebra learning: measurement + angles/polygons + perimeter/circumference + area + scale/similarity + right triangles/distance + surface area/volume + coordinate design/error + mastery
unit.tool_integration: Scientific calculator, geometry games/labs, drawing/tracing tools, and CAD-style resources may support construction and verification after students label diagrams, show formulas, preserve units, and explain constraints.
unit.readiness_note: Unit 11 develops practical geometry and measurement reasoning for learners of any age. Advancement is based on demonstrated mastery, not grade identity.

lessons.title: Measurement Systems, Units & Precision
objectives: Choose appropriate measurement units and tools.
Convert within and between common measurement systems.
Use conversion factors and dimensional analysis.
Distinguish precision, accuracy, estimation, and tolerance.
warmup: Convert 2.5 metres to centimetres.
Name a reasonable unit for the mass of a textbook.
Explain why 4.0 cm communicates different precision from 4 cm.

concepts.heading: Units give numbers meaning
concepts.body: A measurement combines a numerical value with a unit. A bare number cannot communicate length, mass, capacity, or time.

concepts.heading: Conversion factors equal one
concepts.body: A conversion factor is a ratio of equivalent measures, so multiplying by it changes the unit without changing the quantity.

concepts.heading: Precision is not the same as accuracy
concepts.body: Precision describes measurement detail or repeatability; accuracy describes closeness to an accepted or true value.

examples.problem: Convert 3.6 m to cm.

pathways.Foundation: Use labelled conversion strips, measuring tools, and one-step unit ratios.
pathways.Core: Convert measurements, interpret precision, and justify suitable units.
pathways.Extended: Analyze compound conversions, tolerance intervals, percent error, and unit consistency.

lessons.application: Measure or use fictional dimensions for a room, artwork, garden, package, or science sample. Record the tool, unit, precision, and one possible source of error.

lessons.title: Angles, Lines, Transversals & Polygons
objectives: Classify angles and use complementary and supplementary relationships.

warmup: Find the complement of 38°.
Find the supplement of 125°.

concepts.heading: Angle relationships create equations
concepts.body: Complementary angles total 90°, supplementary angles total 180°, and vertical angles have equal measure.

concepts.heading: Parallel lines preserve patterns
concepts.body: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal while same-side interior angles are supplementary.

concepts.heading: Polygon sums grow predictably
concepts.body: An n-sided polygon can be divided into n−2 triangles, so its interior-angle sum is (n−2)·180°.

examples.problem: One angle in a linear pair is 128°. Find the other.

pathways.Core: Write and solve equations from angle and polygon relationships.
pathways.Extended: Derive polygon formulas and analyze parallel-line converses and multi-step diagrams.

lessons.application: Inspect a public building, road marking, artwork, window grid, or fictional design. Identify parallel, perpendicular, complementary, supplementary, or polygon relationships.

lessons.title: Perimeter, Circumference & Composite Boundaries
objectives: Calculate perimeter of polygons and composite figures.
Use radius, diameter, and π to calculate circumference.
Distinguish exterior boundary from shared interior edges.
Estimate and check boundary measurements with units.
warmup: Find the perimeter of a 6 cm by 9 cm rectangle.
Relate the radius and diameter of a circle.
Explain why an interior shared edge is not counted twice in an outside boundary.

concepts.heading: Perimeter follows the outside boundary
concepts.body: Add every exterior side exactly once. Shared interior edges are not part of the outside boundary.

concepts.heading: Circumference is circular perimeter
concepts.body: Use C=πd or C=2πr. Keep an exact answer in terms of π when possible.

concepts.heading: Units stay linear
concepts.body: Perimeter and circumference use units such as centimetres or metres, not square units.

pathways.Extended: Derive missing sides, compare exact and approximate circumference, and optimize boundaries.

lessons.title: Area of Polygons, Circles & Composite Figures
objectives: Calculate area of triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles.
Decompose and recombine composite figures.

Estimate area and evaluate reasonableness.
warmup: Find the area of a 7 by 9 rectangle.
Explain why triangle area is half of a related parallelogram.
Name the height needed in a trapezoid formula.

concepts.heading: Area measures coverage
concepts.body: Area counts two-dimensional square units, so both dimensions must use compatible units.

concepts.heading: Height is perpendicular
concepts.body: In triangle, parallelogram, and trapezoid formulas, height is the perpendicular distance between bases or from a base to the opposite vertex.

concepts.heading: Composite figures can be decomposed
concepts.body: Split a complex region into familiar shapes, or subtract a missing region from a larger shape.

pathways.Extended: Derive formulas, compare decompositions, and solve area constraints backwards.

lessons.title: Scale Drawings, Similarity & Dilations
objectives: Interpret and use scale drawings and map scales.
Identify corresponding sides in similar figures.
Use scale factors and proportions to find missing measures.
Predict how scale affects perimeter and area.
warmup: A drawing uses 1 cm:50 cm. What does 4 cm represent?
State the scale factor from side 6 to side 15.
Explain why doubling length does not merely double area.

concepts.heading: Scale connects a model to reality
concepts.body: A scale states a constant ratio between drawing dimensions and actual dimensions. Units must be made compatible.

concepts.heading: Similar figures preserve shape
concepts.body: Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding side lengths share one scale factor.

concepts.heading: Area changes by the square of scale
concepts.body: If all lengths are multiplied by k, perimeter is multiplied by k and area is multiplied by k².

examples.problem: A floor plan uses 1 cm:50 cm. A wall is 6 cm on the plan.

pathways.Core: Solve scale drawings, similarity proportions, and perimeter/area scale effects.
pathways.Extended: Analyze indirect measurements, coordinate dilations, precision, and compound scales.

lessons.application: Create or inspect a floor plan, map, artwork enlargement, model, blueprint, or fictional habitat plan. State scale, units, and accuracy limits.

lessons.title: Right Triangles, Pythagorean Theorem & Distance
objectives: Use the Pythagorean theorem to find missing right-triangle sides.
Identify legs and hypotenuse correctly.
Use coordinate differences to calculate distance.
Check whether side lengths form a right triangle.
warmup: Identify the hypotenuse in a right triangle.

Find the horizontal and vertical changes from (1,2) to (7,10).

concepts.heading: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle
concepts.body: For a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a²+b²=c².

concepts.heading: Distance creates a right triangle
concepts.body: Horizontal and vertical coordinate changes form perpendicular legs, so distance follows the Pythagorean theorem.

concepts.heading: The converse tests right triangles
concepts.body: If the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right.

pathways.Extended: Use radicals, derive the distance formula, and analyze precision in measured diagonals.

lessons.title: Surface Area, Nets & Volume
objectives: Interpret and construct nets of common solids.
Calculate surface area of prisms and cylinders.
Calculate volume using base area and height.
Distinguish square and cubic units in context.
warmup: Name the units for surface area and volume.
Find the volume of a 2×3×5 rectangular prism.
Describe what a net shows.

concepts.heading: Surface area covers every exterior face
concepts.body: A net unfolds a solid so each face can be measured once. Surface area uses square units.

concepts.heading: Volume fills three-dimensional space
concepts.body: For prisms and cylinders, volume equals base area multiplied by perpendicular height.

concepts.heading: Units reveal the dimension
concepts.body: Length uses units, area uses square units, and volume uses cubic units.

examples.problem: Find volume of a 4×3×2 rectangular prism.

lessons.title: Coordinate Geometry, Design Constraints & Measurement Error
objectives: Use midpoint, distance, and transformations in coordinate designs.

concepts.heading: Coordinates support geometric design
concepts.body: Midpoint, distance, and transformations locate, compare, and reproduce geometric features precisely.

concepts.heading: Measurements carry uncertainty
concepts.body: A measured value is an approximation. Tolerance and error statements communicate acceptable or observed differences.

concepts.heading: A defensible design states constraints
concepts.body: Good geometric models identify units, scale, assumptions, safety or access requirements, rounding, and limitations.
